ety.text: Attested since 1540, origin uncertain. Probably from Low German and Middle Low German lasich (“slack, feeble, lazy”), from las, from Old Saxon lask, from Proto-Germanic *lasiwaz, *laskaz (“feeble, weak”), from Proto-Indo-European *las- (“weak”). Akin to Dutch leuzig (“lazy”), German lässig (“casual, nonchalant, laid-back, easy-going”), Old Norse lasinn (“limpy, tired, weak”), Old English lesu, lysu (“false, evil, base”). More at lush. An alternative etymology traces lazy to Early Modern English laysy, a derivative of lay (plural lays + -y) in the same way that tipsy is derived from tip.

senses.d: Unwilling to do work or make an effort; disinclined to exertion.
ex: Get out of bed, you lazy lout!

senses.d: Causing or characterised by idleness; relaxed or leisurely.
ex: I love staying inside and reading on a lazy Sunday.

senses.d: Showing a lack of effort or care.

ex: We strolled along beside a lazy stream.

senses.d: Of an eye, squinting because of a weakness of the eye muscles.
Turned so that (the letter) is horizontal instead of vertical.
ex: There was probably more cattle bearing the Lazy S brand marketed than those of any other ranch in the world.

senses.d: Employing lazy evaluation; not calculating results until they are immediately required.

ex:
The swilland dropsy enter in
The lazy cuke , and swell his skin

senses.d: To laze, act in a lazy manner.
ex: “Go to sea,” muttered Mr. Unity Peach. “Work for your living—don’t lazy away your time here!”
That same afternoon we were lazying around in a boat among the water-lilies at the edge of the bay.
The “lazies” of the party seized the opportunity of remaining behind—wandering, as they said, though all the cross paths were marked.

ety.text: From feignant, the present participle of feindre (“to fake, to feign”), remotivated by folk etymology in fait (“does”) + néant (“nothing”).

chain.g: backward, slow, dull, lazy, indolent, sluggish, unwilling, motionless, inactive, inert

ety.text: Probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin pigrum. See also peritarsi, which was inherited from a derivative verb pīgritārī.
Inherited from Old Spanish floxo (“loose (thing); weak (person)”), inherited form of Latin fluxus. Doublet of flujo. Compare English flux.
Learned borrowing from Latin inactīvus. By surface analysis, in- + actif.
